newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Rugby Union - Wilson shows why he's the best.
newsitem.headline: Rugby Union - Wilson shows why he's the best.

text.p: MELBOURNE, July 27 - The South Africans blamed Jeff Wilson for their Tri-Nations rugby test loss to the All Blacks last week.
On Saturday night in Melbourne, the Australians said Wilson turned the game on its head for them as well, NZPA reported.

All Blacks coach John Hart privately rates Wilson as the best rugby player in the world at present, and the 23-year-old Dunedin-based Southlander substantiated his coach's belief on Saturday. He produced more magic as the All Blacks wrapped up the Bledisloe Cup series 2-0 with a match to be played, and took a firm grip on the tri-series.

Wilson scored the second All Blacks try within two minutes of the first -- by Frank Bunce -- to give the side a 17-6 lead and take the puff out of the Australians in the first half at the Melbourne Cricket Ground. New Zealand went on to win 33-18 in a match they were never in danger of losing.
Openside flanker Josh Kronfeld stole the ball from Michael Brial and as halfback Justin Marshall straightened up from a run well inside the All Black half, Wilson signalled for an overhead kick.
"I saw (Daniel) Manu there and a lot of open space, and waved to Justin, but I think Justin was going to kick anyway, he read it pretty well," Wilson said.
Wilson chased the perfect punt from Marshall and as the ball bounced up two metres from the line, Wilson dived, clutched the leather and skidded over the line with Joe Roff too late on the scene.
It was a spectacular piece of action that sent the New Zealanders in the 91,000-strong crowd almost crazy with joy. Even the rest of the crowd acknowledged the brilliance of the try.
"Josh has always taken credit for my tries, he quickly told me that he stole the ball," Wilson joked about his Otago and Highlanders' team-mate.
Australian captain John Eales said the try turned the game for Australia.
"When you concede two tries like that in such quick succession it doesn't do much for your enthusiasm," Eales said later.
"I think Jeff's try was the killer blow. We were level and suddenly we were two converted tries down."
The All Blacks were down 23-7 against the Springboks at Ellis Park six days earlier when lethal finisher Wilson struck.

He charged down a kick from halfback Joost van der Westhuizen before the halfway line, picked the ball 40 metres from the line and sprinted around Ruben Kruger. The converted try made it 23-14, and less than two minutes later he popped up on the other wing, accepted a pass and kicked ahead. Carlos Spencer picked it up and closed the gap to 23-19 with a try, allowing the All Blacks to turn the game in the second half.
The Australians were probably thankful that Wilson retired from the game at halftime and was replaced by Adrian Cashmore.

He said he didn't feel well after copping a knee to the head just before halftime. Then another knock from a team-mate during a grid exercise at halftime, which opened a gash on the side of his head, aggravated the effect. He was suffering from a loss of vision temporarily in one eye and a headache.
"I've had it before," Wilson said.
"You get pins and needles in the arms and hands, the lips go twitchy and funny and you get double vision. Ice (Michael Jones) has experienced it before.
"But it's not a worry. The doc (team doctor John Mayhew) checked it out, it's back to normal four or five hours later."
Wilson said he was not concussed and he felt perfectly fine.
The All Black team to play the South Africans in the return tri-series match at Eden Park in two weeks will be named on Tuesday.
No changes are expected.
